In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah [al-Ikhlas] (Sura 112)

This surah is Meccan; this is what Mujahid said, though with a variant report from him, and so did 'Ata' and Qatada. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-'Aliya said: it is Madani.

The Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾ ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten.﴾ ﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham read: "Say: He is Allah, the One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge." Ubayy ibn Ka'b related that "the polytheists asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the lineage of his Lord - exalted is He above what the ignorant say - and so this surah was revealed." Ibn 'Abbas related that "the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: 'O Muhammad, describe your Lord for us and tell us His lineage, for He described Himself in the Torah and gave its lineage.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) trembled until he fell down unconscious, and Jibril (peace be upon them both) descended to him with this surah." Abu al-'Aliya and Qatada said: the factions said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Give us the lineage of your Lord," and so revelation came to him with this surah.

"Ahad" means: One, singular, unique in every aspect of oneness, "there is nothing like unto Him." "Huwa" is the subject (mubtada'), "Allah" is a second subject, and "Ahad" is its predicate; the whole clause is the predicate of the first. It has also been said: "Huwa" is the subject, "Allah" is its predicate, and "Ahad" is an appositive (badal) of it. Abu 'Amr omitted the tanwin from "Ahad" because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), so he read "Allah ahadu Allah," while the others kept it with a kasra because of the meeting of the consonants. As for their pausing, all of them pause with a sukun on the dal. It is related from Abu 'Amr that in continuous recitation (wasl) the dal is sukun, and it is also related from him that it is tanwin.

"Al-Samad" in the speech of the Arabs means: the lord (sayyid) to whom one turns in matters and who is independent in them. They recited:

"Has the mourner not come early with the news of the two best of Banu Asad, 'Amr ibn Mas'ud and the lord al-Samad?"

By this meaning this verse is explained, for Allah, His power be exalted, is the existent of all existents, to Him all turn, by Him they subsist, and none is self-sufficient except Him, glorified and blessed and exalted is He. Many of the exegetes said: al-Samad is the One who has no hollow (jawf), as if it means the solid (al-mus-mat). Al-Sha'bi said: He is the One who neither eats nor drinks. In all of this tafsir there is an objection, for a body is at the furthest remove from Allah the Exalted and from His attributes, so what gives us these expressions?

"Allah al-Samad" is subject and predicate. It has also been said: "al-Samad" is an adjective (na't), and the predicate is what follows.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten.﴾ is a refutation of the allusion of the disbelievers to the lineage about which they asked. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Reflect upon everything, but do not reflect upon the essence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because minds stand short of that, bewildered, while the believers know Allah, the Exalted, through the necessity of His existence, the need of everything for Him, His independence from everything, and reason negates from Him everything unfitting to Him, and that "there is nothing like unto Him." All that I have mentioned is contained within this brief and eloquent surah. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾ means: He has no opposite, no rival, and no equal. "Kufu'" and "kifa'" mean: equal. Nafi', al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "kufuwan" with a damma on the kaf and a softened hamza. 'Asim and Abu 'Amr (in one report from him) read with the hamza. Hamza and Abu 'Amr read "kufan" with the hamza and sukun on the fa'. It is related from Nafi' "kafan" with a fatha on the fa' and without hamza. Sulayman ibn 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas read "wa lam yakun lahu kifa'un" with a kasra on the kaf, a fatha on the fa', and the madd. "Kufuwan" is the predicate of "kana," its subject is "ahad," and the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is cancelled (mulgha). Sibawayh, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, favours that the adverbial phrase, when fronted, be the predicate, but it may come cancelled in places the meaning requires, as in this verse, and as the poet said (Sibawayh recited it):

"As long as there is a young camel calf among them, alive."

It is possible that "kufuwan" is a circumstantial clause (hal) of what precedes, from its being a description of an indefinite noun, as he said:

"For 'Izza, the encampment is desolate..."

Sibawayh said: this is rare in speech; its domain is poetry. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ equals one third of the Qur'an."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because of the tawhid it contains.

The tafsir of Surah [al-Ikhlas] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
